body.p: This Response responds to the Non-Final Office Action dated December 13, 2023.
Claims 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 83, 86, 89, and 90 are presently amended. As a result, claims 20- 25 and 79-92 are now pending in this application.

The undersigned would like to thank Examiner Joseph Tombers for the courtesy of a telephone interview (the "Examiner Interview") on March 14, 2023, which was attended by Applicant's Representative, Joshua Berk (Reg. 73,591). During the Examiner Interview, the rejection of the claims under 35 U.S.C. § 102 was discussed. Proposed claim amendments, which are similar to the claim amendments included herewith, were also discussed.
Claims 20, 22-25 and 79-92 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a) over U.S. 2010/0292557 to Pesach Benny et al. ("Pesach").

an adhesive pad coupled to the sensor mounting unit to adhere the sensor mounting unit to a skin surface of the host;
a heating element included in the adhesive pad and positioned to provide heat to the skin surface of the host when the
implantable analyte sensor is inserted into the host; and

As noted above, claim 20 has been amended to clarify that the sensor electronics hardware of the analyte sensor system detects that the implantable analyte sensor has been inserted into the host by at least receiving a signal indicating a change in an electrical property of the implantable analyte sensor. Claim 20 has been further amended to clarify that in response to receiving the signal indicating the change in the electrical property of the implantable analyte, triggering, the sensor electronics hardware triggers power to be provided to the heating element. As a result, heat is provided to the skin surface of the host upon detection that the implantable analyte sensor has been inserted into the host. Pesach fails to teach or suggest at least these features.

For example, Pesach describes a calibration process in which ISF glucose level is calibrated against serum or blood glucose levels. The calibration protocol "is calibrated at a period of time for example according to one or more of initial use, set frequency, varying frequency, daily, hourly, intermittently, irregular frequency, chaotic frequency, randomized frequency, user defined schedule or the like time frame." See Pesach, para. [0058]. Pesach further generally describes treating the tissue in the vicinity of the sensor's insertion point with heat treatment. For example, paragraph [0060] of Pesach provides that "part of the calibration process of the sensor includes changing the temperature of the tissue in the vicinity of the sensor's insertion point during periods of relatively constant glucose levels." Further, with respect to a method that combines treatment and ISF measurements to increase accuracy of those measurements, paragraph [0191] of Pesach provides that "in stage 1, the sensor is inserted to the body tissue . . . . In stage 2, the ISF glucose data is calibrated with the blood glucose data. In this stage the tissue treatment is [] applied as part of the calibration process to get better accuracy of the sensor's reading and/or shorten the calibration period."

Thus, as discussed during the Examiner Interview, Pesach only generally describes applying a treatment, such as heat, during a calibration process that can take place at various time periods. Pesach fails to disclose specifically triggering the heat treatment in response to detecting insertion of a sensor, and more specifically triggering the heat treatment in response "to receiving the signal
indicating the change in the electrical property of the implantable analyte sensor," as recited by claim 20. Accordingly, claim 20 is allowable over Pesach.

Claim 24 recites, among other things, "a sensor electronics unit installable to the sensor mounting unit, wherein the sensor electronics unit is configured to detect that the implantable analyte sensor has been inserted into the host by at least receiving a signal indicating a change in an electrical property of a contact of the implantable analyte sensor, and begin, in response to receiving the signal indicating the change in the electrical property of the contact of the implantable analyte sensor, providing power to the heating element to heat the skin surface of the host after being installed to the sensor mounting unit, the providing of the power to the heating element being while the implantable analyte sensor is inserted into the host." Claim 83 also recites, among other things, "detecting, by the sensor electronics hardware, that the implantable analyte sensor has been inserted into the host by at least detecting contact between the implantable analyte sensor and the skin surface of the host and/or proximity of the implantable analyte sensor to the skin surface of the host; in response to detecting contact between the implantable analyte sensor and the skin surface of the host and/or proximity of the implantable analyte sensor to the skin surface of the host, providing, by the sensor electronics hardware, power to the heating element, thereby providing heat to the skin surface of the host; and in response to determining that a signal generated by the implantable analyte sensor is substantially linear while the heat is provided to the skin surface of the host, ceasing to provide power to the heating element." Claims 24 and 83 are allowable for at least the same reasons as claim 20.
Claims 22-23, 25, 79-82, and 84-92 depend directly or indirectly from at least one of claims 20, 24, and 83, and are allowable for at least that reason.
The Rejection of Claims Under ? 103
Claim 21 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Pesach in view of U.S. 5918590 to Burkett Timothy Alan ("Burkett").
As amended, claim 21 recites, among other things:
An analyte sensor system comprising:
an implantable analyte sensor configured to be inserted into a host and continuously monitor at least one analyte;
a sensor mounting unit, the implantable analyte sensor coupled to the sensor mounting unit;
an adhesive pad coupled to the sensor mounting unit to adhere the sensor mounting unit to a skin surface of the host;

a heating element included in the adhesive pad and positioned to provide heat to the skin surface of the host when the implantable analyte sensor is inserted into the host, at least a portion of the heating element being positioned outside a perimeter of the sensor mounting unit, and the heating element comprising at least a reactant that reacts in the presence of air to generate heat when the sensor mounting unit is removed from packaging and does not react

when the sensor mounting unit is positioned within the packaging, wherein the adhesive pad comprises a material that permits at least the reactant to have continued exposure to air after the adhesive pad adheres the sensor mounting unit to the skin surface of the host, thereby continuing to provide heat to the skin surface of the host after insertion of the implantable analyte sensor into the
host.

Claim 21 has been amended to clarify that the reactant of the heating element reacts in the presence of air to generate heat when the sensor mounting unit is removed from packaging and does not react when the sensor mounting unit is positioned within the packaging. Claim 21 has also been amended to clarify that the adhesive pad includes a material that permits at least the reactant to have continued exposure to air after the adhesive pad adheres the sensor mounting unit to the skin surface of the host, thereby continuing to provide heat to the skin surface of the host after insertion of the implantable analyte sensor into the host. Pesach, alone, or in combination with Burkett fails to teach or suggest at least these features.

On page 18 of the Office Action, the Examiner acknowledged that Pesach "fails to disclose the first heating element comprising at least a first reactant that reacts in the presence of air to generate heat." To cure the deficiencies in Pesach, the Examiner relied on Burkett. Burkett describes heat cells with oxygen-producing chemical materials. However, Burkett fails to teach or suggest, among other things, "a heating element included in the adhesive pad and positioned to provide heat to the skin surface of the host when the implantable analyte sensor is inserted into the host, . . . the heating element comprising at least a reactant that reacts in the presence of air to generate heat when the sensor mounting unit is removed from packaging and does not react when the sensor mounting unit is positioned within the packaging, wherein the adhesive pad comprises a material that permits at least the reactant to have continued exposure to air after the adhesive pad adheres the sensor mounting

unit to the skin surface of the host, thereby continuing to provide heat to the skin surface of the host after insertion of the implantable analyte sensor into the host," as recited by claim 21. Accordingly, Pesach and Burkett (alone or in combination) fail to teach or suggest all of the limitations of claim 21. Thus, claim 21 is allowable.
Therefore, Applicant respectfully requests the rejections be withdrawn and the claims be allowed.
